“By eight o’clock I had reached a height of seventeen miles above the earth. It seemed clear that I was rising faster and faster, and that a slight increase in speed would have been noticeable even without the ballast I had thrown out. The severe pains in my head and ears returned from time to time, and my nose still bled occasionally. Overall, though, I suffered much less than anyone might have expected. Breathing grew steadily more difficult, and each breath caused an uncomfortable spasm in my chest. I therefore unpacked the condensing equipment and prepared it for immediate use.

“The earth looked truly beautiful at this stage of my ascent. To the west, north, and south, an apparently smooth ocean stretched as far as I could see. Its blue grew deeper every moment, and its surface was already beginning to look slightly curved. Far to the east, but still clearly visible, lay the islands of Great Britain, the whole Atlantic coastline of France and Spain, and a small part of northern Africa. I could no longer make out a single building. Humanity’s proudest cities had vanished completely from the earth’s face. The rock of Gibraltar had shrunk to a faint speck. Beyond it, the dark Mediterranean stretched eastward to the limit of my sight, its shining islands scattered like stars across the heavens. At last, the entire sea seemed to plunge over the edge of the horizon into an abyss. I found myself standing on tiptoe, listening for the echoes of that enormous waterfall. Above me, the sky was pitch-black, and the stars shone brilliantly.

“About this time, the pigeons appeared to be suffering badly, so I decided to set them free. I first untied a beautiful pigeon with grey-mottled feathers and put him on the edge of the wicker basket. He seemed extremely distressed. He looked anxiously about, fluttered his wings, and cooed loudly, but nothing could persuade him to leave the basket. At last I picked him up and threw him about six yards away from the balloon. Instead of flying downward as I had expected, however, he struggled furiously to return, giving sharp, piercing cries as he did so. Eventually he managed to regain his place on the rim. Almost as soon as he reached it, his head sank onto his breast, and he fell dead inside the basket.

But let me warn you in advance that I intend to tell Sybil everything. She is lunching with me tomorrow so that we can discuss bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers a nasty temper, a predisposition to gout, or a wife of yours residing in Bayswater, she shall certainly hear the whole story from me.’

Lord Arthur shook his head with a smile. ‘I have no fears,’ he replied. ‘Sybil understands me quite as well as I understand her.’

‘Ah, I am rather sorry you should say so. Mutual misunderstanding is the sound foundation of matrimony. No, I am not in the least cynical; I simply possess experience, though that amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is longing to have his hand examined. You need not inform him that he is engaged to one of London’s loveliest girls; the Morning Post published that a month since.

‘My dear Lady Windermere,’ exclaimed the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please leave Mr. Podgers with us a little longer. He has just said that I ought to take to the stage, and I find it so fascinating.’

‘If that is what he has told you, Lady Jedburgh, I shall most certainly remove him. Come here immediately, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s palm.’

‘Well,’ Lady Jedburgh remarked, rising from the sofa with a slight pout, ‘if I may not appear on the stage, I must at least be permitted a place in the audience.’

‘Naturally; we shall all be in the audience,’ answered Lady Windermere. ‘Now, Mr. Podgers, make certain you tell us something agreeable. Lord Arthur is a particular favourite of mine.’

At the sight of Lord Arthur’s hand, however, Mr. Podgers turned strangely pale and remained silent. Something like a shiver ran through him, and his thick, enormous eyebrows began twitching with that peculiar, vexing movement which accompanied his perplexity. Great drops of sweat then appeared upon his yellow forehead, resembling a venomous dew, while his plump fingers became clammy and cold.

These unusual symptoms of distress did not escape Lord Arthur, and for the first time he himself knew fear. He felt an urge to flee the room, but mastered it. Whatever the worst might be, knowing it was preferable to enduring this dreadful uncertainty.

‘I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We are all waiting,’ Lady Windermere exclaimed in her brisk, impatient fashion; yet the cheiromantist gave no answer.

‘I suspect Arthur is destined for the stage,’ observed Lady Jedburgh, ‘and after the scolding you gave him, Mr. Podgers dares not say so.’

Dear me, what a champion talker she was. It would scarcely have been proper for me to mention the lateness of the hour, or that I was worn out and desperately sleepy. I regretted not having slipped away to bed while the opportunity offered. Now there was nothing for it but to endure. On and on her voice tinkled through the otherwise deep, spectral silence of the sleeping castle, until at last a distant noise rose, seemingly from far beneath our feet—a stifled shriek, with such anguish in it that my skin crept. The queen broke off, her eyes brightening with delight, and inclined her lovely head like a listening bird. Once more the sound pierced upward through the hush.

‘What is that?’ I asked.

‘Truly, a most obstinate soul, and long enduring. It hath been many hours already.’

‘Enduring what?’

‘The rack. Come, ye shall behold a merry spectacle. If he will not disclose his secret now, ye shall behold him rent apart.’

What a velvet-smooth devil she was, so tranquil and untroubled, while the sinews down my legs ached in fellow-feeling for the man's torment. Armoured guards with blazing torches led us through resounding passages and down wet, dripping stone stairs that smelt of mildew and centuries of captive darkness. It was a lengthy, cold, unearthly journey, neither shortened nor enlivened by the enchantress’s conversation, which concerned the sufferer and his offence. Some nameless informer had charged him with killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

‘Anonymous evidence is hardly satisfactory, your Highness. It would be more just to bring the accuser face to face with the accused.’

‘I had given it no thought, the matter being of little moment. Yet even if I wished it, I could not, for the accuser arrived masked in the night, spoke to the forester, and immediately departed again; thus the forester knoweth him not.’

‘Then this Unknown is the sole witness to the killing of the stag?’

‘Marry, no one witnessed the killing. But this Unknown beheld the stubborn villain close to the place where the stag lay, and out of true loyal ardour came to denounce him to the forester.’

‘So the Unknown was also close to the dead stag? Could he not conceivably have killed it himself? His loyal ardour, behind a mask, seems a trifle questionable. But why does your Highness have the prisoner racked? What is gained by it?’

‘Otherwise he will not confess, and his soul would then be lost. The law requireth his life for his offence—and assuredly I shall see it paid!—but my own soul would be endangered were I to suffer him to die without confession and absolution.
